title: Robinhood Ventures Fund II invests in Opalite Health
summary: Robinhood Ventures Fund II backed Opalite Health in August 2026, supporting faster expansion of AI medical interpretation across health systems.
body_markdown:
###


Robinhood Ventures Fund II is a closed-end Business Development Company listed on the NYSE under the ticker RVII, managed by Robinhood Ventures, a subsidiary of Robinhood Markets. It has invested in Opalite Health as part of a portfolio of roughly 80 private companies, primarily Y Combinator-backed businesses, giving retail investors exposure to early-stage companies before a traditional IPO.


###


No. Opalite remains an independent company, and existing EHR integrations, service commitments, and contract terms are unchanged. The investment adds capital to accelerate roadmap priorities, including expanded language coverage and deeper integrations with Epic, Cerner, and other major systems.


###


Opalite is the right choice for clinical settings. Google Translate is a general consumer tool with no medical terminology optimization, no HIPAA-focused deployment, no encounter documentation, and no healthcare-specific quality controls. Opalite was built for clinical conversations and validated in an independent study with Johns Hopkins Medicine, which found more than 90% fewer major and critical errors compared with certified medical interpreters.


###


Investors cannot buy shares in Opalite directly, but they can purchase shares in RVII, which holds a 1.12% stake in Opalite as part of a diversified portfolio. The RVII IPO is expected on August 13, 2026, priced at $25.00 per share, with the share request window open through August 12, 2026. Review the fund's prospectus and risk disclosures on robinhood.com before requesting shares.


###


Opalite uses healthcare-specific AI trained on millions of minutes of real clinical conversations, with quality controls designed to catch omissions, medication errors, and terminology mistakes in real time. In an independent validation study conducted with Johns Hopkins Medicine, Opalite produced more than 90% fewer major and critical errors compared with certified medical interpreters, though providers should maintain escalation pathways to qualified human interpreters for high-risk encounters such as complex informed consent or end-of-life discussions.
